title: Frequently Asked Questions
subtitle: Privacy model, security practices, and how CipherPay works under the hood.
s1a1: CipherPay uses Zcash shielded transactions exclusively. On the blockchain, all payments are fully encrypted, no outside observer can see the sender, receiver, amount, or memo. However, CipherPay (as the payment processor) does see the transaction details because it performs trial decryption using your viewing key. This is the same trade-off as any payment processor: Stripe sees your transactions too. The difference is that the blockchain layer is completely dark.
s1q2: What data does CipherPay have access to?
s1a2: When using the hosted service, CipherPay can see: your Unified Full Viewing Key (read-only, cannot spend funds), payment amounts, and product names. We cannot see the buyer's wallet balance, other transactions, or identity. We never hold your ZEC — payments go directly to your shielded address. No shipping addresses or buyer PII are stored.
s1q3: How do I get maximum privacy?
s1a3: Self-host CipherPay. The entire codebase is open-source. When you run your own instance, only your server holds the viewing key, and CipherPay (the company) sees nothing. You get the same features — mempool scanning, trial decryption, webhooks, with zero third-party data exposure.
s1a4: No. CipherPay uses a Unified Full Viewing Key (UFVK), which is read-only. It can detect incoming payments but cannot create transactions or move your ZEC. Your spending keys never leave your wallet.
s2q1: Should I use my personal wallet for my store?
s2a1: No. Generate a dedicated wallet exclusively for your CipherPay store. This isolates your commercial transaction history from your personal finances. If the server is ever compromised, an attacker would only see your store's sales history, not your personal net worth or other transactions. Sweep funds from your store wallet to cold storage regularly.
s2q2: What is the recommended wallet setup?
s2a2:
1. Create a brand new wallet (using ZODL, Vizor, zkool, or Zipher (coming soon)) dedicated to your store.
2. Export the Unified Full Viewing Key (UFVK) from that wallet.
3. Use that UFVK when registering on CipherPay.
4. Periodically sweep received funds to your main cold storage wallet.
5. Never reuse this wallet for personal transactions.
s2q3: Can I change my payment address?
s2a3: Yes. You can update your payment address anytime from the dashboard settings. For security, this requires re-entering your dashboard token. New invoices will use the new address. Existing pending invoices keep the address they were created with.
s2q4: Can I change my viewing key (UFVK)?
s2a4: Not in the current version. Changing the UFVK requires the scanner to keep the old key active until all pending invoices are resolved. For now, if you need to rotate your viewing key, create a new merchant account. UFVK rotation is planned for a future release.
s3a1: Each invoice gets a unique payment address derived from your viewing key (UFVK). CipherPay scans the Zcash mempool and new blocks, performing Orchard trial decryption on shielded transactions. When a payment is detected to an invoice's unique address, it is automatically matched — no memo required. This provides sub-minute payment detection, often within seconds.
s3q2: What is the reference code (e.g. CP-C6CDB775)?
s3a2: Each invoice gets a reference code for identification purposes. It is included in the Zcash URI as an informational memo, but payment detection does not depend on it. CipherPay matches payments by their unique cryptographic address, so the buyer just scans the QR code and sends. There is nothing to copy or type.
s3q3: What happens if the buyer sends the wrong amount?
s3a3: CipherPay accepts payments within 0.5% of the invoice price to account for wallet rounding and network fee differences. If a payment is significantly underpaid, it is ignored and the invoice remains pending. The buyer would need to send the correct amount.
s3a4: By default, 30 minutes. This window locks the ZEC/EUR or ZEC/USD exchange rate at the time of invoice creation, protecting both the merchant and buyer from price volatility. If the invoice expires, a new one must be created (with a fresh rate). The expiry duration is configurable via INVOICE_EXPIRY_MINUTES for self-hosted instances.
s4a1: Merchants authenticate via a dashboard token (cpay_dash_...) exchanged for an HttpOnly session cookie. The token is hashed with SHA-256 before storage, a database breach doesn't leak credentials. Sessions use Secure + SameSite=Lax cookies, preventing XSS cookie theft and CSRF attacks. API keys (cpay_sk_...) are also SHA-256 hashed and used for server-to-server integrations.
s4q2: What protections exist against payment exploits?
s4a2: The "penny exploit" (sending 0.00001 ZEC to trigger a confirmation) is blocked by server-side amount verification with a 0.5% slippage tolerance. Webhooks use HMAC-SHA256 signatures with timestamps, preventing both forgery and replay attacks (5-minute replay window). Changing the payment address requires re-authentication with your dashboard token.
s4q3: Does CipherPay store buyer personal data?
s4a3: No. CipherPay does not collect or store shipping addresses, names, or any buyer PII. It is a pure payment processor. Merchants who need shipping information should collect it through their own store and integrate with CipherPay via webhooks for payment confirmation.
s4a4: Yes. CipherPay supports WebAuthn passkeys for passwordless dashboard login. You can register a passkey (Face ID, Touch ID, hardware key) from your dashboard settings. Passkeys are phishing-resistant and never leave your device — CipherPay only stores the public credential, not your biometric data.
s4q5: How do I give an AI agent or service safe API access?
s4a5: Use a restricted API key (cpay_rk_...). Mint one from Dashboard → Settings → Scoped Keys. Restricted keys can create invoices, verify x402, manage agent sessions, and run subscriptions, but cannot change account settings, rotate other keys, settle billing, or delete the account. If a restricted key leaks, the blast radius is limited to your payment operations — not your account. See the API Keys docs for the full deny list.
s5a1: Yes. CipherPay is fully open-source. Clone the repository, configure your environment variables (UFVK, CipherScan API URL, database), and run the Rust binary. It uses SQLite as its database — lightweight and zero-config. PostgreSQL support is planned for a future release.
s5q2: What do I need to self-host?
s5a2: A server with Rust installed (or use the Docker image), access to a CipherScan API instance (public testnet/mainnet endpoints work), and a Zcash wallet to generate your UFVK. The minimum requirements are modest, the Rust binary is lightweight.
s5a3: No. CipherPay has a 1% fee on each payment. Later, subscription tiers with rate limits and premium features are planned. Self-hosting will always remain free.
s5q4: Can I pay for CipherPay with ZEC?
s5a4: That's the plan. When subscription tiers launch, you'll be able to pay for your CipherPay subscription using CipherPay itself, using fully shielded ZEC payments. Dogfooding at its finest.
s6a1: x402 is a protocol that revives the HTTP 402 "Payment Required" status code for programmatic payments. When an AI agent or automated client requests a paid resource, the server responds with 402 and includes payment terms (price, address, chain). The agent pays and retries the request with proof of payment. CipherPay acts as the Zcash facilitator — verifying shielded payments so your server doesn't need to understand Zcash internals.
s6q2: How does verification work for shielded transactions?
s6a2: CipherPay uses the same trial decryption mechanism as invoice detection. When your server calls POST /api/x402/verify with a transaction ID, CipherPay fetches the raw transaction from the Zcash network, attempts to decrypt its Orchard outputs using your viewing key (UFVK), and checks if the decrypted amount meets the expected threshold. The sender's identity remains fully private — only the payment amount and recipient are verified.
s6q3: Does the agent need a CipherPay account?
s6a3: No. The agent just needs a Zcash wallet with funds. It sends ZEC to your payment address and includes the transaction ID in its request. Only the resource server (you) needs a CipherPay account to call the verify endpoint. The agent is completely anonymous.
s6q4: What about payments on other chains?
s6a4: CipherPay is the facilitator for Zcash-to-Zcash payments specifically. For other chains (USDC on Base, ETH, SOL), the resource server would use a different facilitator. The x402 protocol supports multiple chains in the "accepts" array, so a server can offer several payment options. AI agents with multichain wallets (e.g. via NEAR Intents) can swap tokens and pay on whichever chain the server accepts.
s6q5: Is there a fee for x402 verification?
s6a5: No. x402 verification is free. CipherPay provides it to drive Zcash adoption for AI and programmatic payments. Revenue comes from the existing invoice-based payment processing. The x402 facilitator and the invoice checkout system serve different use cases — x402 is for programmatic API access, while invoices are for human-facing e-commerce.
s7q1: Do I need a developer to integrate CipherPay?
s7a1: Not necessarily. If you use Shopify or WooCommerce, install the plugin, enter your API key, and you're live — no code required. For custom integrations, the REST API and SDKs (TypeScript, Python) are straightforward. A single API call creates an invoice and returns a payment link.
s7a2: Yes. Install the CipherPay Shopify app, add your API key in the app settings, and ZEC appears as a payment option at checkout. Orders are automatically marked as paid when the shielded payment confirms. See the docs for setup instructions.
s7a3: Yes. Install the CipherPay WooCommerce plugin, configure your API key under WooCommerce > Settings > Payments, and your WordPress store accepts ZEC. The plugin handles invoice creation, payment detection, and order status updates automatically.
s7q4: What is MCP and how does it work?
s7a4: MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets AI assistants like Claude interact with your CipherPay store directly. Add @cipherpay/mcp to your agent's config, and it can create invoices, check payment status, verify transactions, and manage your store — all through natural language. The agent uses your API key, so it has the same permissions as your server-side integration.
s8a1: You create a product with a recurring price (e.g. $9.99/month). CipherPay generates a new invoice each billing cycle and notifies your server via webhook. The buyer pays each invoice individually — there's no automatic wallet debit, because Zcash doesn't support pull payments. This is by design: the buyer always controls when and how much they send.
s8q2: What happens if a subscriber misses a payment?
s8a2: The invoice expires after the configured window (default 30 minutes). Your webhook receives an expiry notification. How you handle it is up to you — you might send a reminder, pause access, or generate a new invoice. CipherPay doesn't enforce subscription logic; it provides the payment rails.
s8a3: USD, EUR, GBP, BRL, CAD, JPY, MXN, ARS, NGN, CHF, and INR. Prices are set in fiat, and CipherPay converts to ZEC at the current exchange rate when the invoice is created. The rate is locked for the invoice duration.
s9q1: Which Zcash wallets work with CipherPay?
s9a1: Any wallet that supports Zcash Unified Addresses and Orchard shielded transactions. Recommended: ZODL (iOS/Android), Vizor (macOS/Windows/Linux), zkool (iOS/Android/desktop), or Zipher (coming soon). The wallet needs to support scanning QR codes or opening zcash: URIs.
s9q2: Can I test before going live?
s9a2: Yes. CipherPay supports Zcash testnet. Register with a testnet viewing key, and all invoices are created on testnet. You can test the full flow — invoice creation, payment, confirmation, webhooks — without spending real ZEC. When ready for mainnet, register a new merchant account with a mainnet viewing key.
s9q3: Can I accept ZEC in person (point of sale)?
s9a3: Yes. The dashboard includes a POS mode that generates QR codes for in-person payments. The buyer scans, pays, and you see the confirmation in real-time. No card reader, no terminal — just a screen showing a QR code.
s10a1: Zcash shielded transactions are final — there are no chargebacks. This protects merchants from fraud chargebacks, a major pain point with traditional payments. For refunds: at checkout, the buyer can optionally provide a shielded refund address. If they do, the merchant can send ZEC directly to that address from their wallet. If they don't, the buyer keeps maximum privacy but refund requires out-of-band coordination. CipherPay provides the refund tracking UI (mark invoice as refunded, record refund txid) but never holds or moves funds — it's non-custodial. The tradeoff is explicit: chargebacks are replaced by voluntary refund coordination, which is better for merchants (finality, no fraud) and can be better for buyers (no bank intermediary deciding disputes).
s10q2: What if I lose my dashboard access?
s10a2: If you set a recovery email in your dashboard settings, you can reset your access token via the recovery flow. If you didn't set one, there's no way to recover access — CipherPay doesn't store your credentials in a recoverable form (they're hashed). Your funds are safe regardless, since CipherPay never holds your ZEC.
s10a3: Yes. Every component — the Rust backend, the web dashboard, the Shopify app, the WooCommerce plugin, the x402 middleware, the MCP server — is open-source on GitHub. You can audit the code, self-host, or contribute.
s10a4: MPP enables prepaid sessions for high-frequency API access. Instead of paying per-request, an agent deposits ZEC upfront and gets a session token. Each request deducts from the balance. This is more efficient for agents making many small requests — one on-chain transaction covers hundreds of API calls.
s10q5: How do refunds work for AI agent payments?
s10a5: AI agents using Zipher can include a shielded return address in the transaction memo when paying. If included, the merchant has a refund path while the transaction stays fully shielded on-chain. If omitted, the payment has maximum privacy but no automatic refund route. The agent operator chooses this tradeoff. For session-based payments (MPP), unused balance can be refunded to a pre-specified address when the session closes. For x402 payments, refunds are typically unnecessary since the agent only pays for what it receives.
